slides.narration: Welcome to thermodynamics. It is the study of energy changes, and it begins by choosing a part of the universe to watch. That part is the system. Everything else is the surroundings. What we can say about the system depends on what is allowed to cross the boundary between them.

slides.heading: System, surroundings and boundary
slides.body_md: The **system** is the part under study; the **surroundings** are everything else that can exchange energy or matter with it; the **boundary** separates them. System + surroundings = **universe**. A system is **open**, **closed** or **isolated**, according to what crosses the boundary.

rows: Sealed bottle of cola in a fridge
Tea in a stoppered vacuum flask (approximately)

visual.alt: Table of open, closed and isolated systems with what each exchanges and an example

slides.narration: The boundary may be real, like the glass of a flask, or imaginary. An open system exchanges both matter and energy. A closed system exchanges energy only, as heat or work. An isolated system exchanges neither. A perfect isolated system does not exist, but a good vacuum flask is close.

slides.heading: Classifying everyday systems
slides.body_md: Always decide **what the system is** first, then ask whether **matter** or **energy** can cross its boundary. The same object can be a different system depending on what you choose.

rows: Water boiling in an open pan
Sealed ampoule of medicine on a warm shelf
Hot coffee in a sealed vacuum flask
Very little heat or matter crosses

visual.alt: Table of four systems classified as open, closed or isolated with reasons

slides.narration: Always start by naming the system. Boiling water in an open pan is open, because steam leaves and heat enters. A sealed ampoule is closed, because heat crosses but nothing leaves. Hot coffee in a sealed vacuum flask is nearly isolated. A living cell is open, since it exchanges water, gases and energy.

slides.heading: Intensive and extensive properties
slides.body_md: An **extensive** property depends on the **amount** of matter (mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity). An **intensive** property does not (temperature, pressure, density, molar volume, specific heat). A ratio of two extensive properties, such as $\text{mass}/\text{volume}$, is intensive.

slides.heading: Worked example: classify the properties
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A chemist heats 100 g of water in a beaker, then doubles the sample to 200 g at the same temperature. Which of these change? Mass, temperature, density, enthalpy, molar heat capacity, volume.

Doubling the amount **doubles** the extensive properties: mass, enthalpy, volume. It leaves the **intensive** ones unchanged: temperature, density and molar heat capacity (a property per mole).

visual.alt: Table classifying six properties as extensive or intensive with the effect of doubling the sample

slides.narration: Doubling the sample doubles every extensive property. Mass, volume and enthalpy all double. Intensive properties do not depend on the amount, so temperature, density and molar heat capacity stay the same. A property measured per mole or per gram is always intensive.

slides.heading: Quick check: classifying a system
slides.body_md: Decide what can cross the boundary of the system.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look at the situation in the question and decide whether matter, energy, both or neither can cross the boundary of the system. Then choose the type of system that matches.

slides.heading: State of a system and state functions
slides.body_md: The **state** of a system is fixed by its measurable properties: $p$, $V$, $T$ and amount ($n$). A **state function** depends only on the **present state**, not on how it was reached, so its change depends only on the initial and final states. Examples: $U$, $H$, $p$, $V$, $T$. **Heat $q$ and work $w$** are not state functions: they depend on the **path**.

slides.narration: A state function has a value fixed by the present state alone. Its change between two states is the same however you get there. Pressure, volume, temperature, internal energy and enthalpy are state functions. Heat and work are not. They describe how energy is transferred, and they depend on the path taken.

slides.heading: State functions and path functions compared
slides.body_md: On the graph, the **same two end states** are joined by two routes. The change in internal energy is the same on both; the **work** is the area under each route and **differs**.

rows: Cool at 2.0 L, then expand at 1.0 atm
Expand at 4.0 atm, then cool at 6.0 L

visual.alt: Table comparing work on two paths between the same states

slides.narration: Both routes start at the same state and end at the same state. On the first route the gas expands at a low pressure, and little work is done. On the second it expands at a high pressure, and much more work is done. The change in internal energy is identical, because it is a state function.

slides.heading: Thermodynamic processes
slides.body_md: A **process** takes a system from one state to another. It is named by the **quantity held constant**: **isothermal** (T), **isobaric** (p), **isochoric** (V), **adiabatic** (no heat exchanged, q = 0). A **cyclic** process returns to the starting state.

slides.body_md: Read the condition, then name the process. The same table also gives the **simplification of the first law**.

slides.narration: Name the process from what stays constant. Isothermal means constant temperature. Isobaric means constant pressure, and the heat absorbed is the enthalpy change. Isochoric means constant volume, so no pressure volume work. Adiabatic means no heat exchange. In a cyclic process the system returns to its start.

slides.heading: Reversible and irreversible processes; equilibrium
slides.body_md: A **reversible** process is carried out **infinitely slowly**, so the system is in equilibrium at every stage and the driving force is only infinitesimally larger than the opposing force; it can be reversed by an infinitesimal change. Every **real** (spontaneous) process is **irreversible**. A system is in **thermodynamic equilibrium** when it is in thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium.

visual.alt: Table comparing reversible and irreversible processes

slides.narration: A reversible process is an ideal limit. It runs infinitely slowly, with the system in equilibrium at every stage, and the driving force only a whisker larger than the opposing force. All real processes are irreversible. Equilibrium means thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium together.

slides.body_md: What does adiabatic tell you about heat?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall what the word adiabatic says about heat flow, and think about whether that is the same as saying the temperature is constant. Decide whether the statement is true or false.

slides.heading: The first law and its sign convention
slides.body_md: The **first law**: energy can be neither created nor destroyed; the **internal energy $U$** of a system changes only through heat and work. $$\Delta U = q + w$$ **Sign convention used here:** $q > 0$ when heat flows **into** the system; $w > 0$ when work is done **on** the system. So an expanding gas has $w < 0$.

slides.narration: This is the first law of thermodynamics. The change in internal energy equals heat plus work. We count energy flowing into the system as positive, and energy flowing out as negative. Work done on the system, such as compression, is positive. Work done by the system, such as expansion, is negative.

slides.heading: Special cases of the first law
slides.body_md: Combine the law with the process conditions. **Isolated system:** q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔU = 0: the internal energy of an isolated system is constant. **Cyclic process:** ΔU = 0 because U is a state function and the final state is the initial state, so q = −w.

rows: U constant (energy of the universe is constant)
Net heat absorbed = net work done by the system
ΔU = 0; heat absorbed does expansion work

visual.alt: Table of special cases of the first law

slides.narration: In an isolated system nothing crosses the boundary, so internal energy stays constant. In a cyclic process the system comes back to its start, and since internal energy is a state function, its change is zero. So the heat absorbed over the cycle equals the work done by the system.

slides.heading: Worked example: adiabatic expansion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two moles of an ideal gas with $C_V = 12.5\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ expand adiabatically and do 500 J of work. Find $\Delta U$ and the change in temperature.

Adiabatic: $q = 0$. Work is done **by** the gas, so $w = -500$ J. $\Delta U = q + w = 0 + (-500) = -500$ J.

$\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T$, so $\Delta T = \dfrac{-500}{2 \times 12.5} = -20.0$ K: the gas **cools** by 20 K.

visual.alt: Table of q, w, change in internal energy and temperature change in an adiabatic expansion

slides.narration: In an adiabatic change, no heat is exchanged, so the change in internal energy equals the work. The gas does work, so the internal energy falls by five hundred joules. Dividing by the number of moles and the heat capacity at constant volume gives a temperature fall of twenty kelvin.

slides.body_md: Over one complete cycle the system returns to its start, so $\Delta U = 0$ and $q = -w$. On a p–V graph, the **net work equals the area enclosed** by the loop. A clockwise loop means **net work done by the gas**: here 6.0 L atm, or 608 J.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Open systems exchange matter and energy; closed systems energy only; isolated systems neither.
Extensive properties depend on the amount (mass, V, U, H); intensive ones do not (T, p, density). A ratio of extensive properties is intensive.
State functions (U, H, p, V, T) depend only on the states; q and w are path functions.
Process names: isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, adiabatic (q = 0), cyclic (ΔU = 0); real processes are irreversible.
First law: ΔU = q + w, with q and w positive when energy enters the system; ΔU = 0 for isolated and cyclic systems.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Systems are open, closed or isolated. Extensive properties depend on the amount, intensive ones do not. State functions depend only on the states, while heat and work depend on the path. The first law says the change in internal energy equals heat plus work, and it is zero for a cycle.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: State your sign convention before using the first law: q positive into the system, w positive when work is done on the system.
Work done BY a gas in expansion goes into the equation as a negative number.
Always name the system before classifying it as open, closed or isolated.
Say "state function: depends only on initial and final states" and give two examples.
Adiabatic means q = 0, not constant temperature.

rows: Writing ΔU = q − w without saying the convention
Use ΔU = q + w and state that w is on the system
Heat and work are path functions

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. A gas that pushes a piston does pressure volume work, and the amount of work depends on how the expansion is carried out. We calculate it for different routes, then introduce enthalpy and heat capacity, two quantities that chemists use constantly.

slides.heading: Work of expansion against a constant external pressure
slides.body_md: For a gas pushing against a **constant external pressure** $p_\text{ext}$, with volume changing by $\Delta V = V_2 - V_1$: $$w = -p_\text{ext}\,\Delta V$$ The minus sign makes $w$ negative for expansion (work **by** the gas), positive for compression. Units: $1\ \text{L atm} = 101.3\ \text{J}$. In **free expansion** into a vacuum $p_\text{ext} = 0$, so $w = 0$.

visual.alt: Table of the sign of work for expansion, compression, free expansion and constant volume

slides.narration: Work against a constant external pressure is minus the pressure times the change in volume. Expansion gives a negative work, because the gas does the work. In a free expansion into a vacuum, the external pressure is zero, so no work is done. One litre atmosphere is about one hundred and one joules.

slides.heading: Reversible isothermal work
slides.body_md: In a **reversible** isothermal expansion of an ideal gas the external pressure is always only infinitesimally less than the gas pressure. Integrating gives $$w_\text{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\frac{V_2}{V_1} = -2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\frac{p_1}{p_2}$$ For an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$ at constant $T$, so $q = -w$: the gas **absorbs** as much heat as the work it does.

visual.alt: Table of ΔU, w and q for a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas

slides.narration: For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the work is minus two point three zero three times n R T times the logarithm of the volume ratio. The temperature is constant, so the internal energy does not change, and the heat absorbed exactly equals the work done by the gas.

slides.heading: Worked example: irreversible expansion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A gas in a cylinder expands from 1 L to 4 L against a constant external pressure of 2.5 atm. Find the work done on the gas in joules.

$\Delta V = 4 - 1 = 3.0$ L. $w = -p_\text{ext}\Delta V = -2.5 \times 3.0 = -7.5$ L atm.

$w = -7.5 \times 101.3 = -760$ J (negative: the gas does the work).

visual.alt: Table of the steps in an irreversible work calculation

slides.narration: First find the change in volume, which is three litres. Multiply by the external pressure and put in the minus sign for expansion. That gives minus seven point five litre atmospheres. Multiplying by one hundred and one point three converts it to about minus seven hundred and sixty joules.

slides.heading: Worked example: reversible isothermal expansion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two moles of an ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 4 L to 20 L. Find $w$ and $q$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)

$\log_{10}(20/4) = \log_{10} 5 = 0.699$.

$w = -2.303 \times 2 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times 0.699 = -8030$ J. Since $\Delta U = 0$, $q = +8030$ J.

visual.alt: Table of w, q and change in internal energy for the reversible isothermal expansion

slides.narration: The volume ratio is five, and its common logarithm is point six nine nine. Substituting into the reversible work formula gives a work of about minus eight thousand joules. The internal energy does not change at constant temperature, so the gas absorbs the same amount of heat from the surroundings.

slides.heading: Quick check: work against a constant pressure
slides.body_md: Find ΔV, multiply by the external pressure, and attach the sign.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work out the change in volume, multiply by the constant external pressure, and give the work the correct sign. Remember that a gas pushing out against the surroundings does negative work in our convention.

slides.heading: Reversible against irreversible work on a p–V graph
slides.body_md: Work is the **area under the p–V curve**. A gas expanding from 8.0 atm to 2.0 atm at 300 K delivers **1871 J** in one step, **2495 J** in two steps, and the **maximum 3458 J** if reversible. Reversible work is the greatest because the gas always pushes against nearly its own pressure.

slides.heading: Why reversible work is the maximum
slides.body_md: In the **one-step** expansion the opposing pressure is the low final value for the whole change, so the area is small. The **reversible** path keeps the opposing pressure just below the gas pressure at every volume, so the area under the curve is the **largest possible**. For compression the reverse holds: the **reversible path needs the least work**.

visual.alt: Table of work obtained from the one-step, two-step and reversible expansion

slides.narration: In a single step the opposing pressure is low from the start, so the area under the graph is small. A reversible path always keeps the opposing pressure just below the gas pressure, and gets the largest area. For compression the opposite is true, and the reversible path needs the least work.

slides.heading: Enthalpy
slides.body_md: **Enthalpy** is defined as $H = U + pV$. It is a **state function** (U, p and V are) and **extensive**. At constant pressure the only work is $p\Delta V$, so the heat absorbed is $q_p = \Delta U + p\Delta V = \Delta H$. At constant volume, $q_V = \Delta U$.

slides.narration: Enthalpy is the internal energy plus pressure times volume. It is a state function. At constant volume the heat measured is the change in internal energy. At constant pressure, a part of the heat goes into the expansion work, and the heat measured is the change in enthalpy.

slides.heading: Relation between ΔH and ΔU
slides.body_md: For gases treated as ideal, $p\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT$, so $$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g\,RT$$ where $\Delta n_g$ = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. Solids and liquids contribute almost no $p\Delta V$. If $\Delta n_g = 0$, $\Delta H = \Delta U$.

visual.alt: Table of four reactions with the change in moles of gas and the comparison of enthalpy and internal energy changes

slides.narration: For ideal gases, pressure times the volume change equals the change in moles of gas times R T. So the enthalpy change equals the internal energy change plus that term. Count only gaseous substances. If the moles of gas do not change, the two are equal, and solids and liquids hardly matter.

slides.heading: Worked example: from ΔU to ΔH
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 298 K, $\Delta U = -112$ kJ (given). Find $\Delta H$.

$\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$. $\Delta n_g RT = (-1) \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \times 298 = -2.48$ kJ.

$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT = -112 + (-2.48) = -114.5$ kJ.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from internal energy change to enthalpy change

slides.narration: Count the gases. Two product moles minus three reactant moles gives minus one. Multiply by R T, taking care to convert joules to kilojoules, to get minus two point four eight kilojoules. Adding that to the internal energy change gives an enthalpy change of about minus one hundred and fourteen point five kilojoules.

slides.body_md: Count the moles of gas on each side.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count only the gaseous substances on each side of the equation, find the change in the number of moles of gas, and use it to decide how the enthalpy change compares with the internal energy change.

slides.heading: Heat capacity and specific heat
slides.body_md: **Heat capacity** $C$ is the heat needed to raise the temperature of a given sample by 1 K: $q = C\Delta T$ (J K⁻¹, extensive). **Specific heat** $c$ is per gram: $q = mc\Delta T$ (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). **Molar heat capacity** $C_m$ is per mole: $q = nC_m\Delta T$ (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). $c$ and $C_m$ are intensive.

visual.alt: Table of heat capacity, specific heat and molar heat capacity with units

slides.narration: Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of a whole sample by one kelvin, so it depends on the amount. Specific heat is the same per gram, and molar heat capacity is the same per mole. Those two do not depend on the amount, and they characterise the substance.

slides.heading: Heat capacity at constant volume and constant pressure
slides.body_md: A gas can be heated at **constant volume** ($q_V = nC_V\Delta T$) or at **constant pressure** ($q_p = nC_p\Delta T$). At constant pressure it also expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same $\Delta T$: $C_p > C_V$. For one mole of a monatomic ideal gas the gap after 100 K is $R\Delta T = 831$ J.

slides.narration: Both lines start at zero. At constant volume all of the heat raises the internal energy, so the line is lower. At constant pressure the gas also expands, so extra heat is needed for the same temperature rise. The gap between the two lines is the expansion work, R times the temperature change.

slides.heading: C_V, ΔU and the relation C_p − C_V = R
slides.body_md: For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ for **any** process (not only at constant volume). Since $H = U + pV = U + RT$ per mole, $\dfrac{dH}{dT} = \dfrac{dU}{dT} + R$, that is $$C_p - C_V = R$$ (8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). The extra heat at constant pressure is the work $p\Delta V = R\Delta T$.

visual.alt: Table of the expressions for internal energy change, enthalpy change and heats with heat capacities

slides.narration: For an ideal gas the internal energy depends on temperature alone, so the change in internal energy is n times the heat capacity at constant volume times the temperature change, whatever the process. Differentiating enthalpy with respect to temperature shows that the two heat capacities differ by R.

slides.heading: Worked example: heating at constant V and at constant p
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two moles of an ideal gas with $C_V = 20.8\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ are heated by 40 K. Find $q_V$, $q_p$ and the work at constant pressure.

$C_p = C_V + R = 20.8 + 8.314 = 29.1$. $q_V = \Delta U = 2 \times 20.8 \times 40 = 1664$ J. $q_p = 2 \times 29.1 \times 40 = 2329$ J.

$w = \Delta U - q_p = 1664 - 2329 = -665$ J $= -nR\Delta T$.

visual.alt: Table of heats and work for heating an ideal gas at constant volume and at constant pressure

slides.narration: First add R to the heat capacity at constant volume to get the heat capacity at constant pressure. At constant volume the heat equals the internal energy change. At constant pressure more heat is needed. The difference between the two is the work of expansion, which is minus n R times the temperature change.

slides.heading: Quick check: why Cp is larger
slides.body_md: Where does the extra heat go at constant pressure?
slides.narration: Quick check. Read both statements carefully. Decide whether each is true, and then whether the second one is the reason for the first, thinking about where the extra heat goes when a gas is heated at constant pressure.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Work against constant pressure: w = −p_ext ΔV (1 L atm = 101.3 J); free expansion has w = 0.
Reversible isothermal work of an ideal gas: w = −2.303 nRT log(V₂/V₁), q = −w; it is the maximum work.
Enthalpy H = U + pV; q_p = ΔH and q_V = ΔU; ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
q = mcΔT = CΔT; ΔU = n C_V ΔT for an ideal gas; C_p − C_V = R.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part Two. Work against a constant pressure is minus pressure times the volume change. Reversible isothermal work is the largest, and equals the area under the isotherm. Enthalpy is the heat at constant pressure, and differs from the internal energy change by the change in moles of gas times R T. The heat capacities differ by R.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Convert L atm to J with 101.3 before comparing with kJ or J answers; write R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when R is in joules.
In ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT count only gases and convert RT to kJ if ΔU is in kJ.
For reversible work use 2.303 and log to base 10; the ratio is V₂/V₁ or p₁/p₂.
Say clearly: reversible work is the maximum because p_ext differs from p_gas only infinitesimally.
ΔU = n C_V ΔT even when the heating is at constant pressure.

rows: Counting solids and liquids in Δn_g
ΔU uses C_V, ΔH uses C_p

slides.narration: Some exam tips for Part Two. Convert litre atmospheres to joules before you combine them with other energies. Count only gases when you find the change in moles. Use the common logarithm with two point three zero three for reversible work. And remember that internal energy change always uses the heat capacity at constant volume.

sections.heading: 1. System, surroundings and the types of system
sections.body_md:
**Thermodynamics** studies the energy changes that accompany physical and chemical changes. The part of the universe under study is the **system**; everything else that can exchange energy or matter with it is the **surroundings**; the **boundary** separates them (real or imaginary). System + surroundings = **universe**.

- **Open system:** exchanges **matter and energy** (water boiling in an uncovered pan; a living cell).
- **Closed system:** exchanges **energy only** (a sealed bottle; a stoppered flask of ethanol).
- **Isolated system:** exchanges **neither** (a stoppered vacuum flask, to a good approximation).

Always name the system first. The universe as a whole is isolated.

key_terms.definition_md: The part of the universe chosen for study.
Everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it.
A system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.

sections.heading: 2. Properties and state functions
sections.body_md:
The **state** of a system is defined by its measurable properties ($p$, $V$, $T$, $n$). **Extensive** properties depend on the **amount** of matter (mass, volume, $U$, $H$, heat capacity); **intensive** properties do not (temperature, pressure, density, molar volume, specific heat). The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.

A **state function** depends only on the **present state**: its change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path ($U$, $H$, $p$, $V$, $T$). **Heat $q$ and work $w$** are **path functions**. For a cycle, the change in any state function is zero.

key_terms.definition_md: A property that depends on the amount of matter present.
A property that does not depend on the amount of matter present.
A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states of the system.
A quantity (heat or work) whose value depends on how the change is carried out.

sections.heading: 3. Thermodynamic processes; reversible and irreversible changes
sections.body_md:
A **process** takes the system from one state to another. It is named by what is held constant:

- **Isothermal:** $T$ constant ($\Delta T = 0$; for an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$).
- **Isobaric:** $p$ constant; the heat absorbed equals $\Delta H$.
- **Isochoric:** $V$ constant; $w = 0$ (no $p$–$V$ work), so $\Delta U = q$.
- **Adiabatic:** no heat exchanged, $q = 0$, so $\Delta U = w$.
- **Cyclic:** the system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U = 0$ and $q = -w$.

A **reversible** process is carried out **infinitely slowly**, the system being in equilibrium at every stage and the driving force only infinitesimally greater than the opposing force; it gives the **maximum work**. All **real** processes are **irreversible**. **Thermodynamic equilibrium** needs thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium together.

key_terms.definition_md: A process in which no heat is exchanged between the system and the surroundings (q = 0).
A process carried out infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, which can be reversed by an infinitesimal change.
A process in which the system returns to its initial state.

sections.heading: 4. The first law of thermodynamics
sections.body_md:
**Statement:** energy can be neither created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another. The **internal energy** $U$ of a system (the total of all kinetic and potential energies of its particles) changes only through heat and work: $$\Delta U = q + w$$

**Sign convention (used throughout):** $q > 0$ when heat is **absorbed by** the system; $q < 0$ when it is **released**. $w > 0$ when work is done **on** the system (compression); $w < 0$ when the system does work (expansion).

- **Isolated system:** $q = 0$, $w = 0$, so $\Delta U = 0$: the internal energy of an isolated system is constant.
- **Cyclic process:** $U$ is a state function, so $\Delta U = 0$ and $q = -w$.
- **Adiabatic:** $\Delta U = w$; compression warms, expansion cools.

key_terms.definition_md: The total energy of a system: the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its particles.
ΔU = q + w: energy is conserved.

sections.heading: 5. Work of expansion: irreversible and reversible
sections.body_md:
For expansion against a constant external pressure: $$w = -p_\text{ext}\,\Delta V\qquad (1\ \text{L atm} = 101.3\ \text{J})$$ The sign is negative for expansion, and $w = 0$ for free expansion ($p_\text{ext} = 0$) and at constant volume.

For a **reversible isothermal** expansion of an ideal gas: $$w_\text{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\frac{V_2}{V_1}\qquad \Delta U = 0,\ q = -w$$ Work is the **area under the p–V curve**. For 1.00 mol at 300 K expanding from 8.0 atm to 2.0 atm: one step -1871 J, two steps -2495 J, reversible -3458 J. **The reversible path delivers the maximum work**, because the opposing pressure is always nearly the gas pressure; the more steps, the nearer the work gets to the reversible value. For compression the reversible path needs the **minimum** work.

key_terms.definition_md: Work done by or on a gas as its volume changes against an external pressure: w = −p_ext ΔV.
Expansion into a vacuum, with p_ext = 0 and so w = 0.

sections.heading: 6. Enthalpy, heat capacity and the relation C_p − C_V = R
sections.body_md:
**Enthalpy** $H = U + pV$ is an extensive state function. At constant pressure $q_p = \Delta H$; at constant volume $q_V = \Delta U$. For ideal gases $p\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT$, so $$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g\,RT$$ where $\Delta n_g$ is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants (convert $RT$ to kJ if $\Delta U$ is in kJ). $\Delta n_g = 0$ gives $\Delta H = \Delta U$.

**Heat capacity** $C$ (J K⁻¹; $q = C\Delta T$), **specific heat** $c$ (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; $q = mc\Delta T$), **molar heat capacity** $C_m$ (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). For an ideal gas $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ for any process and $\Delta H = nC_p\Delta T$. From $H = U + RT$ per mole: $$C_p - C_V = R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$ At constant pressure the extra heat does the expansion work $p\Delta V = R\Delta T$. For a monatomic gas $C_V = 3R/2 = 12.5$ and $C_p = 5R/2 = 20.8$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using ΔU = q − w without saying which convention is used: here ΔU = q + w and w is positive when work is done on the system.
- Forgetting the minus sign in w = −p_ext ΔV, so an expanding gas gets a positive w.
- Treating adiabatic as isothermal, or calling heat and work state functions.
- Mixing L atm, J and kJ: 1 L atm = 101.3 J; convert Δn_g RT to kJ if ΔU is in kJ.
- Counting solids and liquids in Δn_g, or using C_p for ΔU of an ideal gas.

**Marks**
- First law numericals: signs of q and w (1), substitution (1), answer with unit (1).
- Work of expansion: ΔV (1), formula and sign (1), unit conversion and answer (1).
- Derivations: starting relation (1), key step (1), result (1).

cards.front_md: What is a thermodynamic system?
cards.back_md: The part of the universe chosen for study; the rest is the surroundings.

cards.front_md: Open, closed and isolated systems?
cards.back_md: Open: matter and energy exchanged; closed: energy only; isolated: neither.

cards.front_md: Name the type: a sealed bottle of cola.
cards.back_md: Closed: heat crosses the glass but no matter does.

cards.front_md: Extensive property: definition and two examples?
cards.back_md: Depends on the amount of matter: mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy.

cards.front_md: Intensive property: definition and two examples?
cards.back_md: Does not depend on the amount: temperature, pressure, density, specific heat.

cards.front_md: Is the ratio of two extensive properties extensive or intensive?
cards.back_md: Intensive, because the amount cancels (for example density).

cards.front_md: What is a state function?
cards.back_md: A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path.

cards.front_md: Which of U, H, q, w are state functions?
cards.back_md: U and H are state functions; q and w are path functions.

cards.front_md: What is an isothermal process?
cards.back_md: One in which the temperature of the system stays constant (ΔT = 0).

cards.front_md: What is an adiabatic process?
cards.back_md: One in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (q = 0).

cards.front_md: Isobaric and isochoric processes?
cards.back_md: Constant pressure and constant volume.

cards.front_md: First law for an isochoric process?
cards.back_md: w = 0 (no p–V work), so ΔU = q.

cards.front_md: What is a reversible process?
cards.back_md: One carried out infinitely slowly through equilibrium states, reversible by an infinitesimal change.

cards.front_md: Why are all real processes irreversible?
cards.back_md: They occur at a finite rate with a finite driving force, so the system is not in equilibrium at every stage.

cards.front_md: What is a cyclic process?
cards.back_md: One in which the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0.

cards.front_md: State the first law with its sign convention.
cards.back_md: ΔU = q + w; q positive when heat enters, w positive when work is done on the system.

cards.front_md: What is internal energy?
cards.back_md: The total of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles of the system.

cards.front_md: First law for an isolated system?
cards.back_md: q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔU = 0: its internal energy is constant.

cards.front_md: First law for an adiabatic change?
cards.back_md: ΔU = w: compression warms the gas and expansion cools it.

cards.front_md: Why is ΔU = 0 for a cyclic process?
cards.back_md: U is a state function and the final state is the initial state, so q = −w.

cards.front_md: Work of expansion against a constant external pressure?
cards.back_md: $w = -p_\text{ext}\,\Delta V$; negative for expansion.

cards.front_md: Work in free expansion?
cards.back_md: Zero, because p_ext = 0.

cards.front_md: Convert L atm to joules.
Reversible isothermal work of an ideal gas?
Which expansion gives the maximum work?
cards.back_md: The reversible one: p_ext stays almost equal to the gas pressure.

cards.front_md: What does the area under a p–V curve represent?
cards.back_md: The magnitude of the work done by or on the gas.

cards.front_md: Define enthalpy.
cards.back_md: H = U + pV, an extensive state function; at constant pressure q_p = ΔH.

cards.front_md: Relation between ΔH and ΔU?
cards.back_md: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$, counting only gases.

cards.front_md: When is ΔH equal to ΔU?
cards.back_md: When Δn_g = 0, or when only solids and liquids are involved.

cards.front_md: Units of heat capacity, specific heat and molar heat capacity?
cards.back_md: J K⁻¹; J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: ΔU of an ideal gas in terms of C_V?
cards.back_md: $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ for any process.

cards.front_md: Why is C_p − C_V = R for an ideal gas?
cards.back_md: At constant pressure the gas also does the expansion work p ΔV = R ΔT per mole, which needs extra heat.

questions.stem_md: A hospital pharmacist stores a sealed, unopened bottle of glucose saline in a refrigerator. If the saline in the bottle is taken as the system, the system is best called:

options.text_md: open, because the cold air of the refrigerator surrounds the bottle
closed, because heat can cross the glass but no matter can
isolated, because the bottle is sealed
open, because heat is exchanged with the refrigerator

questions.solution_md: The glass is sealed, so no matter crosses the boundary, but heat flows freely through it. A system that exchanges energy but not matter is closed — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student boils water in an uncovered steel pan on a gas stove and takes the water in the pan as the system. Which description is correct?

options.text_md: Closed: heat enters from the flame but matter stays in the pan
Isolated: the pan is made of steel
Closed: matter can leave the system only in the form of heat
Open: steam leaves the pan and heat enters from the flame

questions.solution_md: Steam (matter) leaves and heat enters, so both matter and energy cross the boundary: an open system — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A hiker pours hot soup into a vacuum flask and screws the stopper on tightly. For the next hour the soup is taken as the system. Which statement is closest to the truth?

options.text_md: The system is nearly isolated: very little heat and no matter cross the boundary
The system is open, because the soup can be poured out later
The system is closed, because heat flows freely through the vacuum wall
The system is open, because the soup is hotter than the surroundings

questions.solution_md: The vacuum wall prevents conduction and convection and the stopper prevents loss of matter, so almost no heat and no matter cross the boundary. The system is nearly isolated — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chemist divides 500 mL of brine at 25 °C into two equal portions in separate beakers. Which property has the same value for each portion as for the original 500 mL sample?

options.text_md: Density
Mass
Volume
Total heat capacity

questions.solution_md: Mass, volume and heat capacity depend on the amount of brine, so each halves (extensive). Density is a ratio of two extensive properties and does not depend on the amount (intensive) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A gas is taken from the same initial state to the same final state by two different routes, one quick and one slow. Which quantity has exactly the same value for the two routes?

options.text_md: The change in internal energy
The heat absorbed by the gas
The work done on the gas
Both the heat absorbed and the work done

questions.solution_md: Internal energy is a state function, so its change depends only on the initial and final states. Heat and work depend on the route — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A gas goes from state A to state B along route X, absorbing 300 J of heat and doing 120 J of work. Along route Y between the same two states the gas does 200 J of work. How much heat does the gas absorb along route Y?
questions.solution_md: Internal energy is a state function, so ΔU is the same on both routes. Route X: ΔU = q + w = 300 − 120 = 180 J. Route Y: 180 = q + (−200), so q = 180 + 200 = 380 J — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The heat absorbed by a gas in going from one given state to another is the same by every route, because heat is a state function.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Heat is a path function: it depends on the route taken. Only quantities such as U, H, p, V and T are state functions.

questions.stem_md: A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states of the system, and not on the path, is called a ___ function.
questions.solution_md: Such a property is a state function (for example internal energy or enthalpy).

questions.stem_md: The ratio of two extensive properties, such as mass divided by volume, is an ___ property.
questions.solution_md: The amount of substance cancels in the ratio, so the result does not depend on the size of the sample: it is an intensive property.

questions.stem_md: Name the type of system (open, closed or isolated) in each case, with a reason: (a) water boiling in an uncovered pan; (b) a stoppered flask of ethanol warming in the sunshine.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Open: steam (matter) leaves the pan and heat enters, so matter and energy are both exchanged. (b) Closed: the stopper prevents matter from leaving, but heat from the sunshine crosses the glass.

questions.solution_md: Pan: open (matter and energy); flask: closed (energy only).

marking_scheme.step: (a) Open, with matter and energy exchanged
(b) Closed, with energy but no matter exchanged

questions.stem_md: Classify each of the following as an intensive or an extensive property: density, enthalpy, molar volume, mass.

answer.model_answer_md: Density: intensive. Enthalpy: extensive. Molar volume: intensive (volume per mole). Mass: extensive.

questions.solution_md: Density and molar volume intensive; enthalpy and mass extensive.

questions.stem_md: Define a state function. Name one state function and one path function.

answer.model_answer_md: A state function is a property whose value depends only on the present state of the system, so that its change depends only on the initial and final states and not on how the change was brought about. Internal energy (or enthalpy, pressure, volume, temperature) is a state function; heat (or work) is a path function.

questions.solution_md: Depends only on the state, not the path; U or H; q or w.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: depends only on initial and final states, not on the path
One state function and one path function

questions.stem_md:
A student studies a few everyday systems and properties.

(a) Classify each system as open, closed or isolated: (i) a lit candle burning in a room, (ii) a sealed ampoule of vaccine kept in an ice box, (iii) a tightly stoppered vacuum flask of hot water, (iv) a green leaf in sunlight. [2]

(b) Classify each property as intensive or extensive, and as a state function or a path function: temperature, work, enthalpy, density. [2]

(c) State, with a reason, why the heat absorbed by a system cannot be called a state function. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Open: the candle takes in oxygen and gives out gases and heat. (ii) Closed: it exchanges heat with the ice but no matter. (iii) Isolated, to a very good approximation: neither matter nor heat crosses the boundary. (iv) Open: it exchanges gases, water and energy with the surroundings.

(b) Temperature: intensive, state function. Work: depends on the amount and on the path; it is a path function (extensive). Enthalpy: extensive, state function. Density: intensive, state function.

(c) The heat absorbed depends on how the change is carried out (the path); the same initial and final states can be joined by routes in which different amounts of heat are exchanged.

questions.solution_md: Open, closed, isolated, open; classification of four properties; heat depends on the path.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Heat depends on the path, not just the states

questions.stem_md: A sample of gas sealed in a rigid steel cylinder is warmed on a burner. This process is best described as:

options.text_md: isobaric
isochoric
isothermal
adiabatic

questions.solution_md: A rigid cylinder cannot change its volume, so the volume is constant: an isochoric process, in which the gas does no p–V work — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An adiabatic process is one in which the temperature of the system stays constant.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged (q = 0). The temperature usually changes, because work changes the internal energy. Constant temperature is called isothermal.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist pumps a tyre so quickly that no heat escapes from the barrel, and the barrel becomes warm. Taking the air in the barrel as the system, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: q > 0 and w = 0, so ΔU > 0 and the air warms
q = 0 and w > 0, so ΔU > 0 and the air warms
ΔU = 0, because no heat is exchanged
q = 0 and w < 0, so ΔU < 0 and the air cools

questions.solution_md: No heat escapes, so q = 0. The plunger does work on the air, so w is positive. Then ΔU = q + w = w > 0 and the temperature rises — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An engineer models the slow lifting of a piston by removing tiny grains of sand, one at a time, from its top. The expansion is treated as reversible because:

options.text_md: the gas does no work during the expansion
the temperature of the gas falls steadily
the change takes place at constant volume
the opposing pressure is always only infinitesimally smaller than the gas pressure, so the system stays in equilibrium

questions.solution_md: Removing the sand grain by grain keeps the driving force infinitesimal, so the gas is in equilibrium at every stage and the change could be reversed by an infinitesimal change — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A system is said to be in thermodynamic equilibrium when it is simultaneously in:

options.text_md: thermal equilibrium only
mechanical equilibrium and phase equilibrium only
thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium
chemical equilibrium only

questions.solution_md: Thermodynamic equilibrium needs equal temperature throughout (thermal), no unbalanced forces (mechanical) and no net change in composition (chemical) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas is carried round a closed loop on a p–V diagram and finally comes back to its starting state. Which quantity is certainly zero for the complete loop?

options.text_md: The change in internal energy
The heat absorbed
The work done
Both the heat absorbed and the work done

questions.solution_md: Internal energy is a state function, so over a cycle that returns to the initial state its change is zero. Then q = −w, and neither q nor w is zero unless the loop encloses no area — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each laboratory situation with the thermodynamic process it represents.

options.text_md: A tyre pump is squeezed so fast that no heat escapes
Water boils in an open pan at atmospheric pressure
Gas in a sealed rigid can is placed on a stove
Gas in a cylinder is compressed slowly while the cylinder sits in a large water bath

questions.solution_md: No heat exchanged: adiabatic; open to the atmosphere: constant pressure, isobaric; rigid can: constant volume, isochoric; large water bath: constant temperature, isothermal.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an isothermal process and an adiabatic process, stating what is constant or zero in each.

answer.model_answer_md: In an isothermal process the temperature of the system stays constant (ΔT = 0); heat can flow in or out to keep it so. In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (q = 0); the temperature of the system generally changes.

questions.solution_md: Isothermal: T constant, heat may flow; adiabatic: q = 0, T changes.

marking_scheme.step: Isothermal: ΔT = 0, heat can be exchanged

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a reversible process? Why can no real process be exactly reversible?

answer.model_answer_md: A reversible process is carried out infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, with the driving force only infinitesimally greater than the opposing force, so that it can be reversed by an infinitesimal change. A real process proceeds in finite time with a finite driving force, so the system is not in equilibrium at every stage.

questions.solution_md: Infinitely slow, equilibrium at every stage; real processes have finite driving force and finite speed.

marking_scheme.step: Infinitely slow, through equilibrium states, infinitesimal driving force
Real processes: finite driving force and speed, so not reversible

questions.stem_md: A cylinder fitted with a piston holds a gas. Name the process, and give the simplified form of the first law, when (a) the piston is clamped and the gas is heated; (b) the piston moves freely under the constant pressure of the atmosphere while the gas is heated; (c) the cylinder is perfectly insulated and the piston is pushed in.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Isochoric (V constant): no p–V work, so ΔU = q. (b) Isobaric (p constant): the heat absorbed equals the enthalpy change, q = ΔH (and ΔU = q + w with w = −p ΔV). (c) Adiabatic (q = 0): ΔU = w, which is positive, so the gas warms.

questions.solution_md: Isochoric ΔU = q; isobaric q = ΔH; adiabatic ΔU = w.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the change in internal energy is zero for a cyclic process, and write the relation between q and w for one complete cycle.

answer.model_answer_md: Internal energy is a state function, so its change depends only on the initial and final states. In a cyclic process these are the same state, so ΔU = 0. Then ΔU = q + w = 0 gives q = −w: the net heat absorbed equals the net work done by the system.

questions.solution_md: U is a state function and the final state equals the initial state; q = −w.

marking_scheme.step: U is a state function and final state = initial state, so ΔU = 0

questions.stem_md: A student squeezes a gas in a syringe: the plunger does 64 J of work on the gas while the gas gives out 28 J of heat to the room. Using ΔU = q + w, the change in internal energy of the gas is:
questions.solution_md: Work is done on the gas, so w = +64 J. Heat leaves the gas, so q = −28 J. ΔU = q + w = −28 + 64 = +36 J — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A reacting mixture is sealed in a rigid, perfectly insulated vessel, and the contents are taken as the system. The first law for this system gives:

options.text_md: ΔU = q, because the volume is fixed
ΔU = 0, because neither heat nor work crosses the boundary
ΔU = w, because heat cannot cross the walls
ΔU > 0, because the reaction releases energy

questions.solution_md: The vessel is insulated (q = 0) and rigid (w = 0), so the system is isolated and ΔU = q + w = 0. The energy released by the reaction only raises the temperature of the contents — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gas absorbs 560 J of heat from a burner and, in expanding, does 210 J of work on a piston. By how much does the internal energy of the gas change?
questions.solution_md: Heat is absorbed, so q = +560 J. The gas does work, so w = −210 J. ΔU = q + w = 560 − 210 = +350 J — option (c).

questions.stem_md: One mole of an ideal gas in a cylinder, immersed in a large water bath at 310 K, is allowed to expand slowly while its temperature stays at 310 K. Which row gives the correct signs of ΔU, q and w for the gas?
questions.solution_md: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so ΔU = 0. The gas expands, so w < 0. Then q = −w > 0: the gas absorbs heat from the bath — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The internal energy of an isolated system remains constant.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. An isolated system exchanges neither heat nor work with its surroundings, so q = 0, w = 0 and ΔU = 0.

questions.stem_md: Match each situation with the form that the first law takes.

options.text_md: Isolated system
Adiabatic change
Constant volume, no p–V work
Isothermal change of an ideal gas

questions.solution_md: Isolated: ΔU = 0; adiabatic: ΔU = w; constant volume: ΔU = q; isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so q = −w.

questions.stem_md: In a model heat engine, a gas absorbs 820 J of heat from a hot source and releases 530 J to a cold sink during one complete cycle. What is the net work, in joules, done by the gas in one cycle?
questions.solution_md: Net heat absorbed $q = 820 - 530 = 290$ J. For a cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so $q + w = 0$ and $w = -290$ J on the gas. The work done by the gas $= 290$ J.

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = 0 so work done by the gas = 290 J

questions.stem_md: A monatomic ideal gas (C_V = 12.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), 0.5 mol in all, expands adiabatically in a thermally insulated cylinder and does 340 J of work. Calculate the change in its temperature, in kelvin.
questions.solution_md: Adiabatic: $q = 0$, so $\Delta U = w = -340$ J (the gas does the work). With $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$: $\Delta T = \dfrac{-340}{0.5 \times 12.5} = -54.4$ K.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The internal energy of an isolated system remains constant.

**Reason (R):** An isolated system exchanges neither heat nor work with its surroundings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. With q = 0 and w = 0, the first law gives ΔU = 0, so Reason explains Assertion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For the gas in each case, state whether q, w and ΔU are positive, negative or zero: (a) an ideal gas is compressed slowly by a piston while the cylinder stays in a thermostat bath; (b) a gas expands adiabatically against the atmosphere; (c) a gas is heated in a rigid sealed cylinder.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Isothermal compression of an ideal gas: ΔU = 0, w > 0 (work done on the gas), so q < 0 (heat flows out to the bath). (b) Adiabatic expansion: q = 0, w < 0 (the gas does work), so ΔU < 0 and the gas cools. (c) Rigid vessel: w = 0, q > 0, so ΔU = q > 0.

questions.stem_md: A sample of an ideal gas expands rapidly inside a perfectly insulated cylinder, pushing a piston outwards. Using the first law and ΔU = n C_V ΔT, explain why its temperature falls.

answer.model_answer_md: The cylinder is insulated, so the change is adiabatic: q = 0. The gas pushes the piston out, so the gas does work and w is negative. Hence ΔU = q + w = w < 0, the internal energy falls. For an ideal gas ΔU = n C_V ΔT with n and C_V positive, so ΔT is negative: the temperature falls.

questions.solution_md: q = 0, w < 0, so ΔU < 0 and ΔT = ΔU/(n C_V) < 0.

marking_scheme.step: Gas does work: w negative, ΔU = w < 0
ΔU = n C_V ΔT so ΔT < 0

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the first law of thermodynamics and write its mathematical form, stating clearly the sign conventions for q and w. [2]

(b) In one complete cycle a gas absorbs 1.40 kJ of heat from a hot reservoir and gives 0.95 kJ to a cold reservoir. Calculate ΔU for the cycle and the net work, and state whether it is done on or by the gas. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Energy can be neither created nor destroyed: the change in the internal energy of a closed system equals the heat exchanged plus the work done. $\Delta U = q + w$, where $q$ is positive when heat is absorbed by the system and $w$ is positive when work is done on the system.

(b) The final state is the initial state and $U$ is a state function, so $\Delta U = 0$. Net heat absorbed $q = 1.40 - 0.95 = 0.45$ kJ. From $\Delta U = q + w = 0$, $w = -0.45$ kJ. The work is negative, so 0.45 kJ (450 J) of work is done by the gas.

questions.solution_md: First law, ΔU = q + w; ΔU = 0; net w = −0.45 kJ, done by the gas.

marking_scheme.step: (a) ΔU = q + w with the sign convention
(b) Net q = 0.45 kJ and w = −0.45 kJ

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by an adiabatic process, and what form does the first law take for it? [1]

(b) One mole of a monatomic ideal gas (C_V = 12.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) at 300 K is compressed rapidly in an insulated cylinder, the surroundings doing 800 J of work on it. Calculate ΔU, q, the temperature rise and the final temperature. [3]

(c) What would be the sign of ΔU if the same gas expanded adiabatically? Give a reason. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, $q = 0$, so $\Delta U = w$.

(b) $q = 0$ and $w = +800$ J (work done on the gas), so $\Delta U = 800$ J. $\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta U}{nC_V} = \dfrac{800}{1 \times 12.5} = 64.0$ K, so $T_2 = 300 + 64.0 = 364$ K.

(c) $\Delta U$ would be negative: the gas does work ($w < 0$) and $q = 0$, so $\Delta U = w < 0$ and the gas cools.

questions.solution_md: q = 0, ΔU = w = +800 J, ΔT = 64.0 K, T2 = 364 K; expansion gives ΔU < 0.

marking_scheme.step: (c) ΔU negative, since w < 0 and q = 0

questions.stem_md: In a school demonstration, 4 L of gas trapped under a light piston swells to 9 L while the atmosphere pushes back with a steady 1.6 atm. Taking 1 L atm = 101.3 J, the work done on the gas is about:
questions.solution_md: $w = -p_\text{ext}\Delta V = -1.6 \times (9 - 4) = -8.0$ L atm $= -8.0 \times 101.3 = −810 J$. The sign is negative because the gas does the work — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas expands isothermally between the same two states, once in a single step against a constant external pressure and once reversibly. The work done by the gas is:

options.text_md: greater in the single step, because the pressure difference driving the change is larger
greater in the reversible expansion, because the opposing pressure stays close to the gas pressure throughout
the same in both, because the initial and final states are the same
zero in both, because the temperature does not change

questions.solution_md: Work is the area under the p–V curve. In the single step the opposing pressure is the low final pressure, giving a small rectangle. The reversible path keeps p_ext just below the gas pressure, giving the larger area under the isotherm — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gas in a cylinder pushes a piston out against a constant external pressure of 1.5 atm, and its volume grows from 2 L to 5 L. Calculate the work done on the gas in joules. (1 L atm = 101.3 J)
questions.solution_md: $w = -p_\text{ext}\Delta V = -1.5 \times (5 - 2) = -4.5$ L atm $= -4.5 \times 101.3 = -456$ J.

questions.stem_md: The gas in the cylinder of a small air compressor grows in volume from 3 L to 8 L, the opposing pressure staying at 1.2 atm throughout. Calculate the work done on the gas, in joules. (1 L atm = 101.3 J)
questions.solution_md: $\Delta V = 8 - 3 = 5.0$ L. $w = -p_\text{ext}\Delta V = -1.2 \times 5.0 = -6.0$ L atm. In joules: $-6.0 \times 101.3 = -608$ J.

marking_scheme.step: ΔV = 5.0 L and w = −6.0 L atm

questions.stem_md: A research student lets 1.5 mol of an ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at 298 K from 6 L to 24 L. Calculate the work done on the gas, in joules. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

**Assertion (A):** A gas that expands isothermally and reversibly absorbs heat from its surroundings.

**Reason (R):** During an isothermal change of an ideal gas no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: The Assertion is true: ΔU = 0 for the ideal gas and w < 0, so q = −w > 0. The Reason is false: in an isothermal change heat flows in (or out) to hold the temperature constant; it is an adiabatic change that has q = 0 — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an expansion between the same two states, an irreversible process delivers more work than the reversible process.

**Reason (R):** In an irreversible expansion the opposing pressure is always equal to the pressure of the gas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are false. A reversible expansion delivers the maximum work, and it is in the reversible process that the opposing pressure is (nearly) equal to the gas pressure at every stage — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A gas is released into an evacuated, insulated vessel and fills it (free expansion). State the work done and the value of ΔU for an ideal gas, with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: The external pressure is zero, so w = −p_ext ΔV = 0. The vessel is insulated, so q = 0. Therefore ΔU = q + w = 0, and for an ideal gas (U depends only on T) the temperature does not change.

questions.solution_md: p_ext = 0 so w = 0; q = 0; ΔU = 0.

questions.stem_md: A gas is taken from state A (6 atm, 1 L) to state B (2 atm, 4 L) by two routes. Route I: the gas is cooled at 1 L until the pressure is 2 atm, then expanded at 2 atm to 4 L. Route II: it is first expanded at 6 atm to 4 L, then cooled at 4 L to 2 atm. Calculate the work done on the gas along each route in L atm, and say what the results show about work and about the change in internal energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Route I: only the expansion at 2 atm does work: w = −2 × (4 − 1) = -6.0 L atm. Route II: only the expansion at 6 atm does work: w = −6 × (4 − 1) = -18.0 L atm. The work is different for the two routes between the same end states, so work is a path function. The end states are the same, so ΔU (a state function) is the same for both.

questions.solution_md: w(I) = -6.0 L atm; w(II) = -18.0 L atm; work depends on path, ΔU does not.

marking_scheme.step: Work is a path function; ΔU is the same (state function)

questions.stem_md: State three differences between a reversible process and an irreversible process.

answer.model_answer_md: A reversible process proceeds infinitely slowly, an irreversible process at a finite rate. In a reversible process the system is in equilibrium at every stage; in an irreversible process it is not. A reversible process is driven by an infinitesimal difference of force or pressure and can be reversed by an infinitesimal change, while an irreversible one has a finite driving force and cannot. A reversible expansion gives the maximum work; an irreversible one gives less.

questions.solution_md: Speed, equilibrium at every stage, driving force, and work obtained.

marking_scheme.step: Equilibrium at every stage against not
Maximum work against less work (or infinitesimal against finite driving force)

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally from pressure p₁ to a lower pressure p₂. On one p–V graph the one-step expansion against p₂ and the reversible expansion are both drawn from the same starting point. Which area is larger, and why? Say what each area represents.

answer.model_answer_md: In the one-step expansion the opposing pressure is p₂ throughout, so the work is the area of the rectangle of height p₂ under the horizontal line from V₁ to V₂. In the reversible expansion the opposing pressure follows the isotherm pV = constant, and the work is the area under that curve between V₁ and V₂. The isotherm lies above the horizontal line p₂ at every volume before V₂, so the area under it is larger: the reversible expansion gives the maximum work.

questions.solution_md: Area under the isotherm exceeds the rectangle under p₂, so reversible work is larger.

marking_scheme.step: Each area is the magnitude of the work for that route
The isotherm lies above the line at p₂ until V₂
So reversible area (maximum work) is larger

questions.stem_md:
One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K is held at 8 atm in a cylinder and allowed to expand isothermally to 2 atm. (R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ for volumes; R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 1 L atm = 101.3 J)

(a) Calculate the initial and final volumes, and the work done on the gas when it expands in one step against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. [2]

(b) The same change is now carried out in two steps: first against 4 atm until the pressure of the gas has fallen to 4 atm, then against 2 atm. Calculate the total work done on the gas. [1.5]

(c) Calculate the work for the reversible isothermal expansion between the same states, and arrange the three values in order of the work obtained. [1.5]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $V = nRT/p$: $V_1 = \dfrac{1 \times 0.0821 \times 300}{8} = 3.08$ L and $V_2 = \dfrac{0.0821 \times 300}{2} = 12.32$ L. $w = -p_\text{ext}\Delta V = -2 \times (12.32 - 3.08) = -18.5$ L atm $= -1871$ J.

(b) The gas reaches $4$ atm at $V_m = 6.16$ L. Step 1: $w = -4 \times (6.16 - 3.08) = -12.3$ L atm. Step 2: $w = -2 \times (12.32 - 6.16) = -12.3$ L atm. Total $= -24.6$ L atm $= -2495$ J.

(c) $w_\text{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log_{10}(V_2/V_1) = -2.303 \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log_{10}4 = -3458$ J. Work obtained: reversible (3458 J) > two steps (2495 J) > one step (1871 J).

questions.solution_md: One step -1871 J; two steps -2495 J; reversible -3458 J; more steps give more work.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Order reversible > two steps > one step

questions.stem_md: Which of the following reactions has ΔH smaller (more negative) than ΔU at the same temperature?

options.text_md: $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$

questions.solution_md: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. For $\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$, $\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$, so $\Delta H < \Delta U$. The reactions with $\Delta n_g = 0$ have $\Delta H = \Delta U$, and $\Delta n_g = +1$ for the decomposition of calcium carbonate gives $\Delta H > \Delta U$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$ at 300 K, the difference $\Delta H - \Delta U$ is closest to ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$):

options.text_md: 0 kJ

questions.solution_md: Only gases count: products 2 mol, reactants $1 + 3 = 4$ mol, so $\Delta n_g = -2$. $\Delta H - \Delta U = \Delta n_g RT = (-2) \times 8.314 \times 300 = -4988$ J $= -4.99$ kJ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Enthalpy is defined by H = U + pV. Which statement about enthalpy is correct?

options.text_md: It is a path function, because it contains the product pV
It is an intensive state function, because pressure is intensive
Its change equals the heat exchanged at constant volume
It is an extensive state function, and its change at constant pressure equals the heat exchanged

questions.solution_md: U, p and V are state properties, so H is a state function; U and V depend on the amount, so H is extensive. At constant pressure q_p = ΔU + pΔV = ΔH; at constant volume the heat equals ΔU — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A reaction in an open beaker releases 56 kJ as heat to the surroundings while the pressure stays at atmospheric pressure. The 56 kJ of heat transferred equals:

options.text_md: ΔU of the reaction, which is −56 kJ
ΔH of the reaction, which is +56 kJ
zero ΔH, because the pressure is constant
ΔH of the reaction, which is −56 kJ

questions.solution_md: At constant pressure the heat exchanged is the enthalpy change, q_p = ΔH. Heat leaves the system, so ΔH = −56 kJ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One mole of argon (C_V = 12.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, C_p = 20.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) is heated from 300 K to 350 K at constant pressure. Treating it as an ideal gas, the change in its internal energy is:
questions.solution_md: For an ideal gas ΔU = n C_V ΔT whatever the process. ΔU = 1 × 12.5 × 50 = 625 J. (The heat absorbed is n C_p ΔT = 1040 J, which also includes the work of expansion.) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For one mole of an ideal gas, C_p exceeds C_V by 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. This difference represents:

options.text_md: the heat lost to the surroundings by radiation
the extra internal energy stored per kelvin at constant pressure
the work done against the surroundings when one mole expands on being heated by 1 K at constant pressure
the energy needed to overcome the attractions between the molecules

questions.solution_md: At constant pressure the gas expands as it is heated and does work p ΔV = R ΔT, which at ΔT = 1 K per mole is R. This extra heat is the difference C_p − C_V = R — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a rigid sealed vessel, 0.4 mol of an ideal gas absorbs 1200 J of heat and its temperature rises by 100 K. The molar heat capacity of the gas at constant volume is:

options.text_md: 12 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
3000 J mol⁻¹
4.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
30 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

questions.solution_md: The vessel is rigid, so q = ΔU = n C_V ΔT. C_V = q/(n ΔT) = 1200/(0.4 × 100) = 30 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (12 J K⁻¹ is the heat capacity of the whole sample, not per mole.) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a kiln at 1100 K, the decomposition $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$ has $\Delta U = +175.0$ kJ per mole of CaCO₃ (illustrative value, given). Calculate $\Delta H$ in kJ. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: Only the gas counts: $\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = 1$. $\Delta n_g RT = 1 \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \times 1100 = 9.15$ kJ. $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT = 175.0 + 9.15 = 184.1$ kJ.

questions.stem_md: A sealed piston holds 0.5 mol of an ideal gas which is warmed from 300 K to 400 K at the constant pressure of the laboratory. Calculate the work done on the gas, in joules. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: At constant pressure $w = -p\Delta V = -nR\Delta T = -0.5 \times 8.314 \times 100 = -416$ J (the gas expands and does work).

marking_scheme.step: p ΔV = n R ΔT for an ideal gas

questions.stem_md: A student warms 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 65.0 °C in a beaker. Taking the specific heat of water as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the heat absorbed, in kJ.

**Assertion (A):** Enthalpy is a state function.

**Reason (R):** Enthalpy is an extensive property.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Enthalpy is a state function because it is defined from U, p and V, which are all state properties. Being extensive is a separate property and does not explain why it is a state function — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Heating one mole of an ideal gas by 1 K at constant pressure needs R joules more heat than heating it by 1 K at constant volume.

**Reason (R):** At constant pressure part of the heat is used by the gas to push back the surroundings as it expands.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. At constant volume all the heat raises U; at constant pressure the gas also does work p ΔV = R ΔT, which needs the extra R joules — Reason explains Assertion, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The specific heat of a substance is an intensive property.

**Reason (R):** Water has a larger specific heat than most common liquids.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true (water 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). Specific heat is heat per gram per kelvin, so the amount of substance cancels and it is intensive; how large water’s value is has nothing to do with that — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Define enthalpy. Under what condition is the heat absorbed by a system equal to its change in enthalpy?

answer.model_answer_md: Enthalpy is the state function H = U + pV, the sum of the internal energy and the product of pressure and volume. The heat absorbed equals ΔH when the change takes place at constant pressure (with only p–V work).

questions.solution_md: H = U + pV; heat equals ΔH at constant pressure.

questions.stem_md: Why is C_p greater than C_V for a gas, while for a solid the two are almost equal?

answer.model_answer_md: At constant volume all the heat raises the internal energy. At constant pressure a gas expands on heating and does work against the surroundings, so extra heat is needed for the same rise in temperature. A solid expands very little, so almost no p–V work is done and the two heat capacities are nearly equal.

questions.solution_md: Gas does expansion work at constant pressure; a solid hardly expands.

marking_scheme.step: Constant p: extra heat goes into expansion work of the gas
A solid expands very little, so little work and C_p ≈ C_V

questions.stem_md: Find Δn_g for each reaction and state whether ΔH is equal to, greater than or smaller than ΔU at the same temperature: (a) $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) -> 2HI(g)}$; (b) $\ce{2KClO3(s) -> 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g)}$; (c) $\ce{C2H4(g) + H2(g) -> C2H6(g)}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Using ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT with only gases counted: (a) Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU. (b) Δn_g = 3 − 0 = +3, so ΔH > ΔU (by 3RT). (c) Δn_g = 1 − 2 = −1, so ΔH < ΔU (by RT).

questions.solution_md: ΔH = ΔU; ΔH > ΔU; ΔH < ΔU.

questions.stem_md: Starting from H = U + pV, show that the heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure is equal to ΔH. Assume that only pressure–volume work is done.

answer.model_answer_md: At constant pressure, ΔH = ΔU + pΔV. By the first law ΔU = q + w, and for p–V work at constant pressure w = −pΔV, so ΔU = q_p − pΔV. Substituting, ΔH = (q_p − pΔV) + pΔV = q_p. The heat absorbed at constant pressure equals the enthalpy change.

questions.solution_md: ΔH = ΔU + pΔV; ΔU = q_p − pΔV; so ΔH = q_p.

marking_scheme.step: ΔH = ΔU + pΔV at constant p

questions.stem_md: A copper block of mass 200 g (specific heat 0.385 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; molar mass 63.5 g mol⁻¹) absorbs 1.54 kJ of heat. Calculate (a) the heat capacity of the block, (b) its rise in temperature, (c) the molar heat capacity of copper.

(a) Starting from $H = U + pV$, derive the relation $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$ for a reaction involving ideal gases at constant temperature and pressure. [3]

(b) For $\ce{2C2H2(g) + 5O2(g) -> 4CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$ at 298 K, $\Delta H = -2600$ kJ (rounded, given). Calculate $\Delta n_g$ and $\Delta U$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$) [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At constant pressure $\Delta H = \Delta U + p\Delta V$. For gases treated as ideal, $pV = nRT$, so at constant $T$ and $p$, $p\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT$, where $\Delta n_g$ is the change in the number of moles of gas. Hence $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. (Solids and liquids have negligible $p\Delta V$.)

(b) Gaseous products: 4 mol CO₂; gaseous reactants: $2 + 5 = 7$ mol, so $\Delta n_g = 4 - 7 = -3$. $\Delta n_g RT = (-3) \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \times 298 = -7.43$ kJ. $\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT = -2600 - (-7.43) = -2592.6$ kJ.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Show that C_p − C_V = R for one mole of an ideal gas. [3]

(b) 2.0 mol of an ideal gas with C_V = 21 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is heated by 25 K at constant pressure. Calculate the heat absorbed, the change in internal energy and the work done on the gas. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For one mole, $H = U + pV = U + RT$. Differentiating with respect to $T$: $\dfrac{dH}{dT} = \dfrac{dU}{dT} + R$. Since $C_p = dH/dT$ and $C_V = dU/dT$ (for an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$), $C_p - C_V = R$.

(b) $C_p = 21 + 8.314 = 29.31$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. $q_p = nC_p\Delta T = 2.0 \times 29.31 \times 25 = 1466$ J. $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = 2.0 \times 21 \times 25 = 1050$ J. $w = \Delta U - q_p = 1050 - 1466 = -416$ J (work done by the gas, $-nR\Delta T$).
